domain_label: Plated-Jewelry Market — Social-Audience Poll & Survey Instrument Design (IG/TikTok)
purpose: A method for choosing and constructing the correct preference-measurement instrument (single-choice, forced-trade-off/MaxDiff, paired comparison, conjoint, WTP) for a stated jewelry-assortment decision, starting from what the owner's simple 'do you like earrings?' IG/TikTok poll genuinely CAN and CANNOT tell you [FACT], while honoring the hard native-platform poll affordances and never reading a poll percentage as measured demand.
assumptions: the polling decision to be informed is the owner's real one: which jewelry categories/styles to rank so a launch set of ~6 items can be picked (S5 assortment); the instrument is chosen to serve that decision, not the other way round

the audience frame (young women ~18-25, IG/TikTok) is given; WHO answers, giveaway-incentive bias, self-selection, sample size and representativeness are the sibling KB kb2's scope, and paid targeting/reach/cost-per-response are kb3's scope; this KB owns instrument DESIGN only

native IG/TikTok poll mechanics are treated as [FACT] constraints as of 2026-07 (IG Story poll sticker = 2 options; IG quiz sticker = up to 4 options with one keyed 'correct'; IG emoji slider = one-dimensional 0-100; IG question sticker = open text; TikTok removed its native in-app poll sticker ~2022 so TikTok polling is via comment/duet/stitch, in-feed A/B, or an off-platform link), and are re-checked when a platform ships a change

survey-methodology facts (MaxDiff/best-worst scaling, conjoint/CBC, Van Westendorp / Gabor-Granger WTP, acquiescence/social-desirability/satisficing bias, MECE option design, primacy/recency order effects, construct/content validity, test-retest reliability) are cited [FACT] with basis and anchor the KB

every preference number a poll would eventually produce is a signal from responders, tagged [ESTIMATE]/[SIGNAL] with method+confidence, never a fabricated [FACT]; category-liking rates, purchase rates, brand shares and prices are NOT invented here
exclusions: WHO answers and how representative they are: giveaway/incentive-induced bias, self-selection, platform sampling bias, minimum sample size and reading noisy data (that is kb2_incentive_sampling_bias)
running polls through paid IG/TikTok ads: audience targeting, campaign objective, poll creative, cost-per-response and translating ad engagement into a signal (that is kb3_paid_reach_and_signal)
the downstream synthesis that combines the poll signal with market and on-site data into a ranked 6-SKU launch set (that is S5 assortment)

fabricating any market number: category-liking %, purchase rate, gold-plated-vs-solid share, demographic/ethnicity buy-rate, brand share or price — this KB encodes the instrument that would MEASURE such things, not the answers
the legal/platform giveaway, sweepstakes and disclosure rules (kb2), and the materials/finish facts (S2 materials)

competency_questions.question: What decision must the poll inform, and why does naming that decision determine the instrument rather than the reverse?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: DECISION_FIRST_FRAMING states the owner's real decision (rank categories/styles to pick a launch ~6) and the decision-led rule, and INSTRUMENT_DECISION_MATRIX maps each decision type to its instrument

competency_questions.question: What can a simple 'do you like earrings?' single-choice/yes-no IG poll genuinely tell you, and what can it NOT?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: SINGLE_CHOICE_LIMITS states it measures coarse top-of-mind category affect among responders and CANNOT give relative ranking (no forced trade-off), intensity, purchase intent, willingness-to-pay or market size, and MEASUREMENT_TARGET separates affect from demand/behavior

competency_questions.question: Why can't a folder of independent yes/no category polls rank the categories, and which instrument produces a ranking?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: FORCED_TRADEOFF_RANKING explains that independent yes/no lets every category score 'yes' with no ordering and that a forced trade-off is required, and MAXDIFF_BEST_WORST supplies the best-worst-scaling instrument that yields a common-scale ranking

competency_questions.question: What are the question types available and what data type does each yield?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: QUESTION_TYPE_TAXONOMY enumerates closed vs open, single-choice, multi-select/check-all, Likert rating, ranking, paired comparison, MaxDiff/best-worst, constant-sum and VAS/emoji-slider with the data type (nominal/ordinal/interval/ranked) each produces

competency_questions.question: What are the native IG/TikTok poll affordances and how do they bound which instrument is feasible in-app?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: NATIVE_POLL_AFFORDANCES states the IG poll(2)/quiz(<=4)/slider(1D)/question(open) mechanics and TikTok's removed native poll, and PLATFORM_SEQUENCING_DESIGN shows how the binary limit forces sequencing or an off-platform route

competency_questions.question: How do you avoid leading, loaded and double-barreled questions and write mutually-exclusive, exhaustive answer options?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: LEADING_LOADED_QUESTIONS names the leading/loaded/double-barreled/assumption-laden failure modes and OPTION_WORDING_MECE requires MECE, balanced, concrete options with an explicit none/other/opt-out

competency_questions.question: How do answer-option order effects and rating-scale design bias responses, and how are they mitigated?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: OPTION_ORDER_EFFECTS states primacy/recency and the randomization mitigation (and that a native sticker can't randomize), and SCALE_DESIGN covers balance, odd-vs-even midpoint, point count and verbal anchors

competency_questions.question: What response-style biases arise at the instrument level and how does instrument design limit them?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: RESPONSE_STYLE_BIAS names acquiescence, social desirability, satisficing/straight-lining and non-differentiation and links each to an instrument-level control (forced choice, neutral wording, short screens)

competency_questions.question: When is category preference not enough — i.e. when must you decompose into attributes/levels and run conjoint?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: ATTRIBUTE_LEVEL_STRUCTURE decomposes a jewelry offer into attributes (category, style/motif, finish, price band) and levels and states that liking one attribute does not compose into product preference, and CONJOINT_INTRO explains choice-based conjoint estimating part-worths incl price to simulate share

competency_questions.question: How is willingness-to-pay measured, and why can a like-poll never yield a price?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: WTP_INSTRUMENTS names Van Westendorp PSM, Gabor-Granger and CBC's price attribute as the price-specific instruments and MEASUREMENT_TARGET states that an affect/liking poll carries no price information

competency_questions.question: Given the native binary constraint, how do you sequence simple polls or route off-platform to reconstruct a ranking?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: PLATFORM_SEQUENCING_DESIGN designs a funnel of paired comparisons / staged single-choice or an off-platform MaxDiff/conjoint link, and INSTRUMENT_DECISION_MATRIX ties the chosen route back to the decision

competency_questions.question: How do you pretest and validate the instrument before spending reach on it?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: PILOT_COGNITIVE_PRETEST specifies a cognitive-interview / soft-launch pretest for ambiguity and misread options, and VALIDITY_RELIABILITY covers construct/content/face validity and test-retest reliability with a hold-out check

competency_questions.question: How is honesty discipline maintained so a poll percentage is read as a responder signal not measured demand, and what is handed to the sampling/reach and assortment steps?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: HONESTY_LEDGER_POLL separates methodology [FACT] from the [SIGNAL] a poll yields and forbids reading a % as demand/market-size, and INSTRUMENT_HANDOFF delivers the recommended instrument set and its constraints while stopping before sampling (kb2), reach (kb3) and assortment (S5)

glossary.definition: The specific questioning device used to elicit a preference — single-choice, multi-select, Likert rating, ranking, paired comparison, MaxDiff/best-worst, constant-sum, VAS/emoji slider, or a conjoint/CBC card set; each yields a different data type and answers a different decision, so the instrument is selected FROM the decision, never picked because a platform sticker is convenient.

A 'pick one' or yes/no item such as the owner's 'do you like earrings?' It measures coarse top-of-mind affect / unconditional interest in a category among the people who answered [FACT-scope]; it CANNOT rank categories (no forced trade-off), measure intensity, purchase intent, willingness-to-pay or market size, and is prone to acquiescence (yes-saying).

A task that makes each option compete against others so a respondent cannot say 'yes' to everything — ranking, paired comparison, constant-sum, or MaxDiff. It is the only way a preference instrument produces a genuine ordering of categories; independent yes/no items cannot, because every category can independently score high.

A forced-trade-off instrument [FACT-Louviere]: respondents see small balanced subsets of items and pick the BEST and WORST in each; across a balanced incomplete-block design this yields ranked preference scores on a common ratio-like scale, reduces scale-use/acquiescence bias, but needs multiple screens and analysis (counting or hierarchical Bayes) and so cannot live inside a single native 2-option IG sticker.

An instrument [FACT] presenting full-profile product cards varying several attributes (e.g. category x style x finish x price) at once; respondents choose among profiles and the model estimates part-worth utilities including a price attribute, enabling share-of-preference and WTP simulation. Heavier than MaxDiff, off-platform, warranted when the decision is a product CONFIGURATION and price, not a single-attribute ranking.

Price-specific methods [FACT]: Van Westendorp Price Sensitivity Meter (four price-perception questions -> acceptable range), Gabor-Granger (buy-likelihood at ascending prices -> demand curve), or the price attribute inside CBC. A liking/affect poll carries zero price information, so WTP is never inferred from 'do you like earrings?'.

Wording defects that bias answers [FACT]: a leading question steers toward an answer ('Do you love our stunning earrings?'), a loaded question smuggles an assumption, and a double-barreled question asks two things at once ('do you like gold-plated earrings?' conflates finish and category). Each corrupts the signal regardless of sample quality.

Answer options that are Mutually Exclusive and Collectively Exhaustive [FACT-method]: non-overlapping, jointly covering the space, concrete, jargon-free, and including an explicit 'none/other/not sure' opt-out so a respondent who prefers none is not forced into a false choice.

Instrument-level answer tendencies independent of true preference [FACT]: acquiescence (agreeing/yes-saying), social desirability (answering to look good), satisficing/straight-lining (minimal effort, same answer down a list) and non-differentiation; mitigated by forced choice, neutral balanced wording and short screens. (WHO answers and self-selection are kb2's sampling scope, not this.)

The output of even a well-designed poll is a preference SIGNAL from the responders, tagged [SIGNAL]/[ESTIMATE] with method + confidence — never a measured market [FACT]. A category-liking percentage is not a purchase rate, a demand size or a price; those require sampling (kb2), reach (kb3) and prevalence x frequency methods elsewhere.

nodes.definition: Anchor the whole KB in the decision-led rule: name the business decision the poll must inform BEFORE choosing any instrument, because the decision determines the instrument, never the reverse [FACT-method / METHOD]. The owner's real decision is not 'do people like earrings' in the abstract but 'which jewelry categories/styles should the launch ~6 items be, ranked' (feeding S5 assortment). A decision framed as a RANKING implies a forced-trade-off instrument; a decision framed as a single go/no-go implies a binary; a decision about PRICE implies a WTP instrument. Writing the decision, the choice set, and the action each possible result would trigger is the first design act; a poll whose result would not change any action is mis-scoped.

included: naming the decision, choice set and triggered action before instrument choice
the owner's decision as a category/style RANKING for the launch 6
the decision-led (not sticker-led) selection rule

nodes.definition: Enumerate the instrument types and the data type each yields [FACT-survey methodology], the vocabulary the rest of the KB uses. Closed vs open. Closed: single-choice/'pick one' (nominal, one winner, no ordering of the rest); multi-select/check-all-that-apply (nominal, prone to under-report of unchecked items); Likert rating (ordinal intensity per item, but items scored independently); ranking (ordinal order across items); paired comparison (one forced choice between two, aggregates to a scale); MaxDiff/best-worst (ranked common-scale scores); constant-sum (allocate 100 points, interval-like trade-off); VAS/emoji-slider (quasi-interval 0-100 on one dimension). Open: free text (rich, unstructured, hard to aggregate, good for discovery). The data type dictates what statistics and rankings are legitimate downstream; choosing a type that yields nominal data when the decision needs a ranking is the root design error.

included: closed vs open; single-choice, multi-select, Likert, ranking, paired comparison, MaxDiff, constant-sum, VAS
the data type (nominal/ordinal/interval/ranked) each yields
the rule that data type gates legitimate downstream analysis
excluded: which type to pick for a given decision (INSTRUMENT_DECISION_MATRIX)

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a new instrument type or data-type consideration is added

pros.claim: A clean type-to-data-type map lets every later node reason about what a chosen instrument can legitimately produce
pros.example: tagging single-choice as nominal-one-winner makes its inability to rank the losers obvious

cons.claim: The taxonomy is abstract until tied to a decision, so on its own it does not tell the owner what to run
cons.example: listing eight instrument types without the decision map can overwhelm rather than guide

failure_modes: choosing an instrument whose data type cannot support the ranking the decision needs
treating multi-select counts as if unchecked meant 'disliked' rather than 'not top-of-mind'
acceptance_tests: closed/open and the eight named instrument types are listed each with the data type (nominal/ordinal/interval/ranked) it yields and the analysis that data type permits
revisit_triggers: a new instrument type or platform format becomes relevant

nodes.definition: Pin the construct — WHAT is being measured — because different constructs need different instruments and are routinely conflated [FACT]. Distinguish: (a) affect / unconditional liking ('do you like earrings?'); (b) relative preference / trade-off ('earrings vs necklaces vs rings, which most?'); (c) purchase intent ('would you buy?'); (d) willingness-to-pay ('at what price?'); (e) salience / top-of-mind ('what comes to mind?'); (f) behavior / actual past purchase. A like-poll measures only (a) among responders and does NOT license claims about (b)-(f): liking is not preference (everything can be liked), is not intent (liking is cheap, buying is costly), and carries no price. Naming the construct before drafting the item is what prevents 'do you like earrings?' from being over-read as demand.

included: the six distinct constructs (affect, relative preference, purchase intent, WTP, salience, behavior)
the rule that liking is not preference, intent or price
naming the construct before drafting the item
excluded: the mechanics of the limited single-choice item (SINGLE_CHOICE_LIMITS)

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: the target construct for a decision changes

pros.claim: Separating the constructs stops the single most common error of reading a liking % as demand or intent
pros.example: labelling 'do you like earrings?' as affect-only blocks a leap to 'earrings will sell'

cons.claim: Insisting on a single construct per item can feel pedantic when a casual poll seems to answer several at once
cons.example: an owner may want one poll to reveal liking, intent and price together, which no single item can do

failure_modes: conflating liking with purchase intent or demand
inferring a price or a ranking from an item that measured only affect
acceptance_tests: the construct (affect vs relative preference vs intent vs WTP vs salience vs behavior) is named for each item, with the explicit statement that liking is not preference, intent or price
revisit_triggers: the decision changes which construct matters (e.g. moves to price or intent)

nodes.definition: Diagnose the owner's exact instrument — a simple single-choice / yes-no 'do you like earrings?' category poll — CAN and CANNOT tell you [FACT, load-bearing]. CAN: give a coarse top-of-mind affect / unconditional-interest read on ONE category among the self-selected people who answered; a cheap, fast, high-response engagement signal; a rough screen to drop a category almost nobody reacts to. CANNOT: rank categories against each other (no forced trade-off, so earrings, necklaces and rings can each independently score 80%+ 'yes'); measure preference intensity or how much more one is wanted; reveal purchase intent (liking is costless, buying is not) or willingness-to-pay (no price in the item); size the market or 'how many buy' (that needs prevalence x frequency and a representative frame, not a self-selected story audience); or say WHICH earring/style/finish (the category is not a product). It is also biased toward acquiescence (yes-saying) and toward whoever already follows the account. Verdict: a valid instrument for coarse category screening, an invalid one for ranking, intent, price or sizing.

included: the CAN list: coarse single-category affect, cheap high-response signal, drop-a-dead-category screen
the CANNOT list: ranking, intensity, intent, WTP, market size, which product; plus acquiescence bias
the verdict that it screens but does not rank/price/size
excluded: the forced-trade-off instrument that fixes ranking (FORCED_TRADEOFF_RANKING)

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: the like-poll is used beyond coarse category screening

pros.claim: Spelling out the CAN vs CANNOT lets the owner use the easy poll for what it is valid for and stops the over-read
pros.example: using 'do you like earrings?' only to drop a category nobody reacts to, not to decide the launch order

cons.claim: Emphasizing the limits can read as dismissing a cheap high-response tool the owner already likes and can run today
cons.example: an owner may over-correct and abandon a useful coarse screen entirely

failure_modes: reading independent yes-percentages across categories as a ranking
treating a like-% as purchase intent, willingness-to-pay or market size
acceptance_tests: the CAN (coarse single-category affect, cheap screen) and CANNOT (rank, intensity, intent, WTP, size, which product) lists and the acquiescence caveat are stated with the screens-not-ranks verdict
revisit_triggers: the owner starts using a like-poll result to rank or price categories
the decision needs intensity/intent/price the item cannot give

nodes.definition: Establish why a ranking decision needs a forced-trade-off instrument [FACT]. Independent yes/no or independent Likert items score each category on its own, so a friendly audience can rate earrings, necklaces, rings and bracelets all 'yes'/'8-of-10' and produce NO usable ordering — the exact failure of running several 'do you like X?' polls. A forced trade-off makes options compete: ranking (order them), paired comparison (A vs B, repeated), constant-sum (split 100 points), or MaxDiff (best & worst from a subset). Only these yield a genuine ordering and separate a strong from a mild preference. The cost is higher respondent effort and (on native IG/TikTok) the impossibility of doing it in one binary sticker, which is what forces sequencing or an off-platform survey. For the owner's 'which categories to launch' decision, some forced trade-off is mandatory, not optional.

included: why independent items cannot rank and yield all-yes
the four forced-trade-off instruments (rank, paired comparison, constant-sum, MaxDiff)
the effort/native-feasibility cost of forcing a trade-off

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: the ranking requirement or the drop-off tolerance changes

pros.claim: Showing that only a forced trade-off can rank converts a vague 'poll the categories' into a specific instrument requirement
pros.example: replacing four independent yes/no polls with one paired-comparison funnel actually orders the categories

cons.claim: Forced trade-offs cost more respondent effort and can raise drop-off versus a one-tap yes/no
cons.example: asking a story viewer to rank six categories is far more work than tapping 'yes' once

failure_modes: running independent yes/no per category and getting an all-yes non-ranking
assuming independent Likert averages can be compared as a ranking without a trade-off
acceptance_tests: the all-yes failure of independent items and the four forced-trade-off instruments that produce a real ordering are stated, with the effort/native cost named
revisit_triggers: the decision stops needing a ranking (single go/no-go)
respondent drop-off makes a lighter trade-off necessary

nodes.definition: Specify the MaxDiff / best-worst-scaling instrument [FACT-Louviere & Woodworth]: respondents view small balanced subsets (typically 4-5 items) drawn by a balanced incomplete-block design and pick the BEST and the WORST item in each subset; repeated over several subsets this produces ranked preference scores on a common, near-ratio scale, with far less scale-use and acquiescence bias than rating each item (because it is a forced choice, not an agree/disagree). It is the strongest lightweight instrument for ranking the owner's jewelry categories/styles. Costs: it needs multiple screens (not one sticker), a designed block plan for balance, and analysis by counting (best-minus-worst) or hierarchical Bayes for individual-level scores. Consequently it cannot run inside a native 2-option IG poll and must be delivered as a sequence of paired/subset choices or via an off-platform form (Typeform/Sawtooth/Google Form + scoring).

included: best-worst subset mechanics and the balanced incomplete-block design
the common-scale ranked output and reduced scale/acquiescence bias
the multi-screen/off-platform delivery and counting vs hierarchical-Bayes analysis
excluded: how it is sequenced/hosted in practice (PLATFORM_SEQUENCING_DESIGN)

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: the ranking item set or the available MaxDiff tooling changes

pros.claim: MaxDiff yields a clean common-scale ranking with low scale bias, ideal for ordering jewelry categories/styles
pros.example: best-worst over category subsets ranks earrings vs necklaces vs rings on one scale rather than four independent yes-rates

cons.claim: It needs multiple screens, a balanced design and analysis, so it cannot be a one-tap native sticker and raises design and completion cost
cons.example: a proper 8-item MaxDiff may need ~6-8 subset screens, impossible in a single IG poll

failure_modes: attempting MaxDiff inside a single binary sticker and getting an unbalanced, uninterpretable result
skipping the balanced-block design so some items appear far more often and the scores are biased
acceptance_tests: best-worst subset mechanics, the balanced incomplete-block requirement, the common-scale ranked output and the multi-screen/off-platform + counting/HB analysis are all stated
revisit_triggers: the item list to rank grows or shrinks, changing the block design
an off-platform MaxDiff tool becomes available or unavailable

nodes.definition: Catalogue the question-wording defects that corrupt a signal regardless of sample quality [FACT-survey methodology]. Leading: wording that steers ('Do you love our stunning new earrings?' presumes love). Loaded: smuggles an assumption ('Which of our best-selling styles...' presumes best-selling). Double-barreled: two questions in one ('do you like gold-plated earrings?' conflates finish AND category, so a yes is uninterpretable). Emotionally charged or brand-flattering adjectives, presupposition, and framing (gain vs loss) all bias answers. Absolute vs comparative framing matters too ('do you like X?' invites yes-saying; 'X or Y?' forces a comparison). The fix is neutral, single-barreled, presupposition-free wording tested against a reading of 'could this nudge the answer?'. For the owner, 'do you like gold-plated earrings?' must be split into a category item and a separate finish item, or it measures nothing clean.

included: leading, loaded, double-barreled, charged-adjective and framing defects
the absolute-vs-comparative yes-saying issue
splitting a double-barreled category+finish item
excluded: response-set biases like acquiescence at aggregate (RESPONSE_STYLE_BIAS)

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a wording defect or a new bundled-attribute risk appears

pros.claim: A concrete defect catalogue lets a drafter scrub wording before fielding and catch the double-barreled finish+category trap
pros.example: splitting 'do you like gold-plated earrings?' into category and finish items makes both answers interpretable

cons.claim: Perfectly neutral wording can read as dry and lower engagement on a platform that rewards punchy copy
cons.example: a flat 'earrings or necklaces?' may get fewer taps than a playful but leading line

failure_modes: shipping a double-barreled 'gold-plated earrings?' item whose yes cannot be attributed to finish or category
using brand-flattering adjectives that inflate the yes-rate
acceptance_tests: leading, loaded and double-barreled defects are defined with the category+finish split and the neutral-single-barreled fix stated
revisit_triggers: a drafted item bundles two attributes or presupposes an answer
engagement pressure pushes toward punchier leading copy
a new attribute (e.g. price) risks being bundled into a category item

nodes.definition: Design the answer options so the item is answerable and unbiased [FACT-method]. Options must be Mutually Exclusive (no overlap: not '$20 or less' and '$20-$40' both containing $20) and Collectively Exhaustive (cover the space), concrete and jargon-free (say 'studs / hoops / drops', not 'ear adornments'), balanced in valence, and include an explicit opt-out ('none of these / not sure / other') so a respondent who prefers none is not forced into a false preference. Category lists must be at one taxonomic level (don't mix 'earrings' with 'gold hoops'). Too many options invite satisficing; too few force a false dichotomy. For native stickers the 2- or 4-option ceiling means the option SET must be pruned to the most decision-relevant contrasts, or the item split across several polls.

included: mutual exclusivity, exhaustiveness, concreteness, balance and an explicit opt-out
single-taxonomic-level option lists
pruning options to fit the native 2/4 ceiling
excluded: the order the options appear in (OPTION_ORDER_EFFECTS)

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: the option set or a native option ceiling changes

pros.claim: MECE, opt-out-bearing options make each answer interpretable and stop a forced false choice from manufacturing a preference
pros.example: adding 'none of these' reveals when the real answer is that none of the offered categories appeals

cons.claim: An opt-out and exhaustive options can drain responses into 'not sure' and dilute a clean signal
cons.example: a large 'none' bucket may leave too few directional responses to act on

failure_modes: overlapping price/size buckets so a respondent fits two options
omitting an opt-out and forcing a preference from someone who has none
acceptance_tests: options are shown mutually exclusive, exhaustive, concrete, single-level and balanced with an explicit none/other/opt-out, and pruned to any native option ceiling
revisit_triggers: a category/price/finish list changes the option set
responses pile into 'other', signalling a missing option
the native option ceiling forces a re-prune

nodes.definition: Account for answer-order effects [FACT]: option position biases choice — primacy (first options favored in visual/self-administered lists, as on an IG sticker) and recency (last options favored when read aloud), plus anchoring by the first option shown. The standard mitigation is randomizing or systematically rotating option order across respondents so position bias averages out. The complication: native IG/TikTok stickers do NOT let you randomize order, so a fixed-order sticker bakes in a primacy bias toward the top option — a real limit on reading a native two-option poll as if the two were positioned neutrally. Where order cannot be randomized, mitigations are counterbalancing across separate story posts (swap the order on a second post) or moving the item off-platform to a form that can randomize.

included: primacy/recency and first-option anchoring
randomization/rotation as the mitigation
native inability to randomize and the counterbalance-across-posts or off-platform workaround
excluded: the wording/balance of the options themselves (OPTION_WORDING_MECE)

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: native order-randomization support or an order-artifact concern changes

pros.claim: Naming the native no-randomization limit prevents over-reading a fixed-order sticker's top-option lead as true preference
pros.example: swapping option order on a second story post reveals how much of the lead was primacy

cons.claim: Counterbalancing across two posts doubles the fielding effort and splits the audience
cons.example: running each contrast twice with swapped order halves the responses per version

failure_modes: reading a fixed-order sticker's top-option win as a clean preference
failing to counterbalance and attributing a primacy artifact to real liking
acceptance_tests: primacy/recency and first-option anchoring are stated with randomization as the mitigation and the native no-randomize limit plus counterbalance/off-platform workaround
revisit_triggers: a native format adds order randomization
a poll's top option wins by a suspiciously small margin
the item is moved to a form that can randomize

nodes.definition: Construct rating scales correctly when an intensity read is wanted [FACT-survey methodology]: use a balanced scale (equal positive and negative anchors, symmetric labels); decide odd vs even points deliberately — an odd count (5 or 7) offers a neutral midpoint (honest 'no opinion' but a satisficing refuge), an even count forces a lean; 5-7 points is the usual sweet spot (more points add noise not information, fewer lose discrimination); label points verbally not just numerically for shared meaning; and keep one scale direction consistent across items. The IG emoji slider is a 0-100 visual-analog scale on ONE dimension — quasi-interval, good for a single intensity read, useless for comparing separate items or for anything multi-dimensional. A rating scale still scores items independently, so it does not substitute for a forced trade-off when a ranking is the goal.

included: balance, odd-vs-even midpoint, 5-7 point count, verbal anchors, consistent direction
the emoji slider as a one-dimensional VAS
the reminder that independent ratings still cannot rank

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: an intensity-read need or a scale-artifact concern changes

pros.claim: A well-formed balanced 5-7 point scale gives a clean intensity read and prevents mid-point and length artifacts
pros.example: a symmetric 5-point like-scale beats a 0-10 slider that mostly adds noise for a single-item read

cons.claim: A neutral midpoint can become a satisficing refuge and independent ratings still can't be compared as a ranking
cons.example: many respondents parking on the midpoint hides real leanings and yields no ordering

failure_modes: using an unbalanced scale (more positive than negative anchors) that inflates positivity
treating separate Likert averages as a legitimate ranking
acceptance_tests: balance, the odd-vs-even midpoint decision, the 5-7 point range, verbal anchors and the slider-as-1D-VAS are stated with the independent-ratings-cannot-rank caveat
revisit_triggers: an intensity read is needed rather than a ranking
midpoint parking dominates responses
a multi-dimensional construct is forced onto a one-dimensional slider

nodes.definition: Name the response-style biases that live in the instrument itself (distinct from WHO answers, which is kb2's sampling scope) [FACT]. Acquiescence: a tendency to agree / say yes, which inflates every 'do you like X?' item. Social desirability: answering to look good (e.g. over-claiming interest in 'sustainable' or 'premium'). Satisficing / straight-lining: minimal-effort responding — picking the first acceptable option, parking on a midpoint, or giving the same answer down a battery. Non-differentiation: rating everything the same. Extreme/central-tendency response styles skew scales. Instrument-level mitigations: prefer forced choice over agree/disagree (kills acquiescence and non-differentiation), keep items neutral and short (limits satisficing), avoid batteries long enough to invite straight-lining, and include an occasional attention/consistency check. These are why a like-poll's raw yes-rate reads high and why a forced trade-off is more robust.

included: acquiescence, social desirability, satisficing/straight-lining, non-differentiation, extreme/central tendency
instrument-level mitigations (forced choice, neutral short items, attention checks)
why raw like-rates read high
excluded: self-selection and who is in the sample (kb2)

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a response-style artifact or a sensitive attribute appears

pros.claim: Cataloguing instrument-level biases justifies preferring forced choice and short neutral items over agree/disagree batteries
pros.example: switching from 'do you like X?' to a best-worst choice removes the acquiescence inflation entirely

cons.claim: Attention checks and forced choices add friction that can raise drop-off on a casual social poll
cons.example: an extra consistency-check screen may cost completions on a low-commitment story audience

failure_modes: reading an acquiescence-inflated yes-rate as true enthusiasm
letting a long battery invite straight-lining that hides real differences
acceptance_tests: acquiescence, social desirability, satisficing/straight-lining and non-differentiation are named with forced-choice/neutral-short-item mitigations and the raw-like-rate-reads-high point
revisit_triggers: responses show straight-lining or non-differentiation
an item battery grows long enough to invite satisficing
a social-desirability-sensitive attribute is added

nodes.definition: Decompose a jewelry offer into attributes and levels so the right question grain is chosen [FACT/METHOD]. Attributes for this venture: category (studs/hoops/drops, necklace/pendant/choker, ring/band, bracelet/bangle, anklet), style/motif (minimalist, statement, Y2K, etc.), finish (gold-plated, vermeil, gold-filled, rhodium-plated silver, stainless), and price band. Levels are the values within an attribute. The key fact: a preference measured on ONE attribute does not compose into a preference for a PRODUCT that bundles several — liking 'earrings' and liking 'gold' does not tell you the appeal of a specific gold earring at a specific price, because attributes trade off against each other. Choosing the grain (rank categories only? or rank whole product profiles?) determines whether a MaxDiff on one attribute suffices or a conjoint over bundled profiles is required. This is the bridge from single-attribute polling to full product evaluation.

included: the attribute set (category, style, finish, price) and levels
the fact that single-attribute preference does not compose into product preference
grain choice (single-attribute rank vs bundled profile)
excluded: the conjoint instrument that models bundles (CONJOINT_INTRO)

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: the decision grain or the attribute set changes

pros.claim: Explicit attributes/levels reveal when a category ranking is insufficient and a bundled product evaluation is needed
pros.example: seeing category, finish and price as separate attributes shows why 'rank the categories' won't price a specific gold-plated hoop

cons.claim: Full attribute decomposition can over-scope a decision that only needs a coarse category read
cons.example: modelling four attributes when the owner only needs to drop two categories is wasted effort

failure_modes: composing single-attribute likings into an assumed product preference
picking a category-only grain when the decision is actually about a priced product
acceptance_tests: the attribute set (category/style/finish/price) with levels and the non-composability of single-attribute preference into product preference and the grain-choice rule are stated
revisit_triggers: the decision moves from category ranking to a priced product configuration
a new attribute (e.g. metal tone, gemstone) becomes decision-relevant
single-attribute results are being composed into product claims

nodes.definition: Introduce choice-based conjoint (CBC) as the instrument for product-configuration-and-price decisions [FACT-Green & Rao / Sawtooth]: respondents repeatedly choose among full-profile product cards that vary several attributes at once (e.g. category x style x finish x price); a discrete-choice model estimates part-worth utilities per level INCLUDING a price attribute, from which you simulate share-of-preference and price sensitivity for hypothetical products. It answers 'which bundled product, at what price, wins' — which MaxDiff (single-attribute ranking) and a like-poll cannot. Costs: more attributes/levels multiply the design, it needs many choice tasks and enough respondents for stable estimation, and it is strictly off-platform (a Sawtooth/Conjoint.ly/QuestionPro form, never a native sticker). Use it only when the decision is genuinely about a priced product configuration, not the owner's first-order category screen.

included: full-profile choice tasks over multiple attributes incl price
part-worth utilities and share/price simulation
off-platform delivery and the when-warranted (priced product config) rule

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a priced-configuration decision or conjoint tooling changes

pros.claim: Conjoint is the one instrument that jointly models product configuration and price to simulate share, which no single-attribute method can
pros.example: a CBC over category x finish x price predicts which priced hoop beats which priced stud

cons.claim: It is design- and sample-hungry and strictly off-platform, over-scoped for a first category screen
cons.example: a four-attribute CBC needs many tasks and respondents, far beyond an IG story audience's patience

failure_modes: reaching for conjoint when a coarse category screen is all the decision needs
under-powering the design so part-worths are unstable
acceptance_tests: full-profile choice tasks, part-worths incl price, share/price simulation, the off-platform requirement and the priced-product-config warrant are stated
revisit_triggers: the decision becomes a priced product configuration
attributes/levels grow, changing design size
a conjoint platform becomes available or too costly

nodes.definition: Specify the price-specific instruments, because willingness-to-pay is a construct a like-poll cannot touch [FACT]. Van Westendorp Price Sensitivity Meter: four price-perception questions (too cheap / cheap / expensive / too expensive) yield an acceptable price range and points of marginal cheapness/expensiveness — good for a first price-corridor read, weak on actual demand. Gabor-Granger: ask buy-likelihood at ascending price points to trace a demand curve and a revenue-maximizing price — direct but anchoring-prone. CBC's price attribute (see CONJOINT_INTRO): the most realistic because price trades off against real product features. None of these is a native sticker: at most a single Gabor-Granger price point can be A/B'd across two story posts, but a true WTP read is an off-platform form. The rule: if the decision needs a price, use a WTP instrument; never infer price from 'do you like earrings?'.

included: Van Westendorp PSM, Gabor-Granger, CBC price attribute
each method's strength/weakness and off-platform nature
the rule to never infer price from a like-poll

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a price-measurement need or WTP tooling changes

pros.claim: Naming the WTP instruments gives a real way to get price and blocks inventing a price from a liking poll
pros.example: a Gabor-Granger buy-likelihood ladder yields a demand curve where 'do you like earrings?' yields nothing on price

cons.claim: WTP methods are anchoring-prone and off-platform, and stated-price answers overstate real buying
cons.example: Gabor-Granger's ascending prices anchor respondents and inflate stated willingness versus actual purchase

failure_modes: inferring a price from a category like-poll
reading stated WTP as actual demand without a behavioral check
acceptance_tests: Van Westendorp, Gabor-Granger and the CBC price attribute are named with their strengths/limits and the never-infer-price-from-a-like-poll rule
revisit_triggers: the decision needs a price corridor or curve
a stated-WTP result must be validated against behavior
a WTP tool becomes available

nodes.definition: Compose the core deliverable: a map from decision type to instrument [FACT/METHOD]. Single category go/no-go interest -> single-choice/binary (valid only as a coarse screen). Order/rank several categories or styles -> forced trade-off: MaxDiff for many items, ranking or a paired-comparison funnel for few. Pick between two concrete designs -> paired comparison / A/B. Choose a bundled product configuration and its price -> choice-based conjoint. Find a price point/corridor -> Van Westendorp or Gabor-Granger. Open discovery ('what would you want?') -> open-text question sticker. For the owner's stated decision (rank categories/styles to pick a launch 6), the matrix selects a MaxDiff or a sequenced paired-comparison funnel, NOT the independent 'do you like earrings?' polls, and flags any native single-sticker attempt as under-powered. Each mapping records the construct measured and the native-vs-off-platform feasibility.

included: the decision-type -> instrument mappings with construct and feasibility
the owner's ranking decision routed to MaxDiff / paired-comparison funnel
flagging under-powered single-sticker attempts
excluded: who is sampled (kb2) and paid reach (kb3)

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a decision type or an instrument capability changes a mapping

pros.claim: A single decision->instrument matrix makes instrument choice reproducible and routes the owner's decision to the right method
pros.example: the matrix sends 'rank categories for the launch 6' to MaxDiff and rejects four independent yes/no polls

cons.claim: A matrix can oversimplify hybrid decisions that need more than one instrument in sequence
cons.example: a decision needing both a category rank and a price read must chain MaxDiff then Gabor-Granger, not pick one cell

failure_modes: picking the cell for the platform sticker on hand rather than for the decision
mapping a ranking decision to independent single-choice polls
acceptance_tests: the decision-type -> instrument mappings (screen/rank/A-B/config+price/price-point/discovery) with construct and native-vs-off-platform feasibility are stated, and the owner's ranking decision is routed to MaxDiff / paired-comparison
revisit_triggers: the decision type changes or becomes hybrid
a new instrument or native capability changes a mapping
an under-powered single-sticker plan is proposed for a ranking

nodes.definition: Turn the chosen instrument into something the platforms can actually deliver, given the native binary ceiling [METHOD]. Two routes. (1) Sequence simple native items to approximate a richer instrument: a funnel of paired comparisons (earrings vs necklaces, winner vs rings, ...) reconstructs an ordering; a staged screen (category poll, then within the winning category a style A/B, then a finish A/B) drills down; each is a legitimate chain of 2-option stickers. Its cost is that each stage loses and re-selects a different self-selected sub-audience (a bias handed to kb2) and paired-funnel order can affect the outcome. (2) Route off-platform: post a link (link sticker/bio) to a Typeform/Google Form/Sawtooth hosting a true MaxDiff or conjoint, trading reach and completion for instrument rigor. The design act is choosing, per decision, between an approximate native sequence and a rigorous off-platform form, and documenting the trade-off so the downstream sampling/reach KBs inherit it cleanly.

included: paired-comparison funnels and staged native drill-downs
off-platform link-out to MaxDiff/conjoint forms
the native-approximation-vs-off-platform-rigor trade-off and the sub-audience bias handed to kb2
excluded: the sampling bias that the sequencing creates (kb2 analyses it)

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: native mechanics, funnel drop-off, or off-platform feasibility changes

pros.claim: Explicit sequencing/off-platform design lets a rigorous instrument survive the binary native ceiling instead of being abandoned or faked
pros.example: a three-stage paired-comparison funnel orders four categories using only 2-option stickers

cons.claim: Native sequences leak a different sub-audience at each stage and off-platform forms lose reach and completion
cons.example: each funnel stage answered by a different self-selected slice muddies the composite ranking

failure_modes: chaining stages whose changing sub-audiences make the composite ranking incoherent
assuming a native sequence is bias-free when each stage re-selects respondents
acceptance_tests: the paired-comparison-funnel / staged-drill-down native routes and the off-platform link-out are specified with the approximation-vs-rigor trade-off and the per-stage sub-audience bias flagged for kb2
revisit_triggers: native poll mechanics change the feasible sequence
per-stage drop-off makes a funnel incoherent
an off-platform form becomes preferable or infeasible

nodes.definition: Pretest the instrument before spending reach [METHOD]. Cognitive interviewing: have a handful of target-audience members think aloud while answering to expose ambiguous wording, misread options, an unintended reading of 'do you like earrings?' or a double-barreled item that slipped through. Soft launch: run the poll to a small organic slice first, inspect the response distribution for pathologies (near-100% agreement = acquiescence or a leading item; a huge 'other'/opt-out = a missing option; a coin-flip split = no signal or an order artifact) before any paid amplification. Pretesting is cheap relative to buying reach on a broken item; skipping it means paying to collect uninterpretable answers. The output is a revised instrument and a go/no-go to scale.

included: cognitive interviewing to catch ambiguity/misreads
soft-launch distribution diagnostics before paid reach
the revised-instrument + go/no-go output
excluded: the validity/reliability theory behind the checks (VALIDITY_RELIABILITY)

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: an item changes or a soft-launch pathology appears

pros.claim: A cheap pretest catches ambiguous or leading items before money is spent collecting uninterpretable answers
pros.example: a think-aloud reveals respondents read 'do you like earrings?' as 'do you own earrings?', prompting a reword

cons.claim: Pretesting adds a step and a small delay, and a tiny pretest sample can miss rarer misreadings
cons.example: five think-aloud users may not surface a misreading that appears only at scale

failure_modes: buying reach for an un-pretested item and collecting uninterpretable data
ignoring a soft-launch pathology (all-yes, huge opt-out) before scaling
acceptance_tests: a cognitive-interview pretest and a soft-launch distribution check (agreement/opt-out/coin-flip pathologies) precede any paid reach, producing a revised instrument and a scale go/no-go
revisit_triggers: any item wording or option set changes
a soft-launch distribution shows a pathology
a new audience segment could read items differently

nodes.definition: Judge whether the instrument measures the intended construct (validity) and does so consistently (reliability) [FACT-psychometrics]. Validity: face (does it look like it asks the right thing), content (does it cover the construct), construct (does it behave as the construct should — e.g. a preference measure should correlate with a hold-out choice), and criterion (does it predict a relevant behavior, ideally an actual add-to-cart or purchase). Reliability: test-retest (same respondents, similar answers later), internal consistency across related items, and split-half checks. Practical checks for this venture: include a hold-out task (a direct 'if you had to pick one to buy' item) and see whether the MaxDiff ranking predicts it; re-ask a subset to gauge stability. A poll can be perfectly worded yet invalid if it measures affect while the decision needs predicted purchase — validity is judged against the construct named in MEASUREMENT_TARGET, not against how clean the item looks.

included: face/content/construct/criterion validity and test-retest/internal-consistency reliability
a hold-out purchase-intent check against the ranking
validity judged against the named construct not surface cleanliness
excluded: the pretest procedure that operationalizes some checks (PILOT_COGNITIVE_PRETEST)

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a hold-out contradiction or a construct change occurs

pros.claim: Validity/reliability checks catch an instrument that is clean but measures the wrong construct or is unstable
pros.example: a hold-out 'which would you buy' item that contradicts the like-poll ranking exposes an affect-not-intent instrument

cons.claim: Full validity/reliability testing needs extra items and a re-ask, adding respondent burden a casual poll resists
cons.example: a test-retest re-contact is hard on an anonymous story audience

failure_modes: accepting a clean-looking item that measures affect when the decision needs predicted purchase
reporting a ranking without any hold-out or stability check
acceptance_tests: face/content/construct/criterion validity and test-retest/internal-consistency reliability are stated with a hold-out purchase-intent check, and validity is judged against the named construct
revisit_triggers: a hold-out item contradicts the instrument's ranking
the construct of interest changes
a re-ask shows unstable answers

nodes.definition: Enforce the tag discipline so a poll's output is never over-read [honesty contract]. Solid [FACT] (methodology, load-bearing): the native affordance limits; the question-type -> data-type map; that a like-poll gives coarse affect and cannot rank/price/size; that only a forced trade-off ranks; MaxDiff/conjoint/Van Westendorp/Gabor-Granger mechanics; the wording, order and response-style biases; validity/reliability definitions. Soft [SIGNAL]/[ESTIMATE]: every preference number a fielded poll would yield is a signal from the responders with method + confidence, not a measured market fact. [UNKNOWN] until measured/sourced: the actual category-liking rates, purchase rates, gold-plated-vs-solid share, demographic/ethnicity buy-rates, brand shares and prices — this KB builds the instrument that would measure them; it does not supply the answers. The binding rule: a poll percentage is a [SIGNAL] from a self-selected audience, never a demand, market-size or price [FACT]; representativeness that would upgrade the signal is kb2's job.

included: the [FACT] methodology anchors vs the [SIGNAL] poll outputs vs the [UNKNOWN] market numbers
the rule that a poll % is a responder signal not demand/size/price
deferring representativeness to kb2
excluded: the sampling correction that upgrades a signal (kb2)

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a poll output is over-read or a market number is fabricated

pros.claim: A single ledger keeps the methodology trustworthy while forbidding a poll % from being read as measured demand or price
pros.example: tagging a 70% earring-like result as a [SIGNAL] from responders blocks a leap to '70% of the market wants earrings'

cons.claim: Heavy tagging frustrates a stakeholder who wants a single confident market number the evidence cannot support
cons.example: an owner wanting 'the answer' must accept a signal-with-caveats, not a demand figure

failure_modes: promoting a poll [SIGNAL] to a measured demand, market-size or price [FACT]
fabricating a category-liking, ethnicity-buy-rate, brand-share or price number the poll has not measured
acceptance_tests: the [FACT] methodology anchors, the [SIGNAL] poll outputs, and the [UNKNOWN] market numbers are enumerated with the rule that a poll % is never demand/size/price
revisit_triggers: a poll result starts being cited as a market fact
kb2 supplies a representativeness correction that reframes the signal
a fabricated market number appears downstream

nodes.definition: Compose the segment's hand-off: deliver the recommended instrument set for the owner's decision and stop cleanly before sampling, reach and assortment. For 'rank categories/styles to pick a launch 6': recommend an off-platform MaxDiff (or a native paired-comparison funnel if reach must stay in-app), a MECE non-leading option set, a pretested and validity-checked build, and every result carried as a [SIGNAL]. Explicitly NOT included: how many respondents and whether they represent the 18-25 buyer, and how a giveaway/incentive would bias them (kb2); how to run the poll through paid IG/TikTok ads and convert engagement to cost-per-response (kb3); and how to fuse the poll signal with market and on-site data into the final ranked 6 (S5). The binding conditions passed on: choose the instrument from the decision; never read a like-poll as a ranking; pretest before spend; and tag every output a signal, not a fact.

included: the recommended instrument set + option/pretest/validity conditions for the owner's ranking decision
the clean boundary before sampling (kb2), reach (kb3) and assortment (S5)
the four binding design conditions passed on
excluded: paid reach and cost-per-response (kb3); the final ranked launch set (S5)

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: the decision, candidate list, or a downstream KB's needs change the hand-off

pros.claim: A clean hand-off gives the owner a runnable, honest instrument set and names the boundaries without overstepping into sampling or reach
pros.example: handing over a pretested MaxDiff plus 'every result is a signal' lets kb2/kb3 add representativeness and reach on a sound instrument

cons.claim: Stopping before sampling and reach means the hand-off is an instrument, not yet an answer, which can frustrate an owner wanting the ranking now
cons.example: the deliverable is 'how to measure', not 'earrings rank first', which arrives only after fielding

failure_modes: letting the instrument recommendation drift into sampling or reach claims this KB does not own
handing off without the pretest/validity/signal-tag conditions attached
acceptance_tests: the recommended instrument set with option/pretest/validity conditions, the clean pre-sampling/pre-reach/pre-assortment boundary, and the four binding design conditions are stated
revisit_triggers: the owner's decision or candidate list changes the recommended instrument

conflict_axes.name: decision_led_vs_sticker_led
conflict_axes.description: Choosing the instrument from the decision versus grabbing whatever native sticker is convenient; the convenient binary rarely fits a ranking or price decision.
poles: select the instrument from the decision
run whatever native sticker is easy
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: always derive the instrument from the named decision and its construct; treat native convenience as a delivery constraint, not the instrument chooser

conflict_axes.name: simple_binary_ease_vs_forced_tradeoff_rigor
conflict_axes.description: A one-tap yes/no maximizes responses but cannot rank; a forced trade-off ranks but costs effort and drop-off.
poles: maximize responses with an easy binary
get a real ordering with a forced trade-off
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: if the decision is a ranking, accept the forced-trade-off cost; reserve the easy binary for coarse screening only

conflict_axes.name: native_reach_vs_instrument_rigor
conflict_axes.description: Staying in a native sticker keeps reach and completion high but caps the instrument at binary; going off-platform gains MaxDiff/conjoint rigor at the cost of reach.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: match to the decision stakes: coarse screen native, a launch-defining ranking off-platform or via a documented paired-comparison sequence

conflict_axes.name: affect_vs_purchase_and_price
conflict_axes.description: Liking is cheap and easy to measure; purchase intent and willingness-to-pay are what the business needs and neither is inferable from affect.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: name the construct first; never infer intent or price from an affect item, use intent and WTP instruments when the decision needs them

conflict_axes.name: single_attribute_rank_vs_bundled_product
conflict_axes.description: Ranking one attribute (categories) is light and native-approximable; evaluating bundled priced products needs conjoint and is heavy.
poles: rank a single attribute with MaxDiff
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: choose the grain from the decision: category ranking -> MaxDiff, priced product configuration -> conjoint; do not compose single-attribute likings into a product claim

conflict_axes.name: completion_volume_vs_data_quality
conflict_axes.description: Longer, forced, opt-out-bearing instruments yield richer, cleaner data but raise drop-off; short easy items yield more but noisier responses.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: keep items as short as the decision allows, use forced choice for quality, and pretest drop-off before scaling

conflict_axes.name: neutral_wording_vs_engaging_nudge
conflict_axes.description: Neutral balanced wording protects validity but a punchy leading line drives more taps on a social feed.
poles: make copy punchy even if leading
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: hold neutrality on the measured item; put the personality in surrounding creative, not in the question stem or options

conflict_axes.name: fixed_order_sticker_vs_order_control
conflict_axes.description: Native stickers show a fixed option order that bakes in primacy bias, while validity wants randomized or counterbalanced order.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: counterbalance order across posts or move off-platform when the margin is small enough that primacy could flip it

conflict_axes.name: open_discovery_vs_closed_precision
conflict_axes.description: Open-text discovers unanticipated preferences but is hard to aggregate; closed options are precise but only within the options offered.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: use open-text early to discover the option space, then closed MECE items to measure it; do not skip discovery and hard-code options that miss the real preference

conflict_axes.name: point_estimate_vs_signal_honesty
conflict_axes.description: Stakeholders want one confident number while the evidence supports only a responder signal with caveats.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: report the result as a [SIGNAL] from responders with method and confidence; never promote a poll % to a measured demand, share or price

edge_cases.description: The owner runs a single 'do you like earrings?' yes/no and reads 80% yes as 'earrings will sell', treating affect as demand with no trade-off and no baseline
edge_cases.trigger: a like-poll result is read as purchase demand or a ranking
edge_cases.mitigation: report the result as coarse affect among responders only; use a forced trade-off for ranking and an intent/WTP instrument for demand/price

edge_cases.description: Each category is polled with its own independent yes/no, and every category scores 80%+, producing no usable ordering for the launch 6
edge_cases.trigger: independent binary items are used to rank multiple categories
edge_cases.mitigation: replace independent yes/no with a forced trade-off (MaxDiff or a paired-comparison funnel) that makes categories compete

edge_cases.description: A double-barreled item 'do you like gold-plated earrings?' conflates finish and category, so a yes cannot be attributed to either
edge_cases.trigger: two attributes are bundled into one question
edge_cases.mitigation: split into a category item and a separate finish item, or model both via conjoint

edge_cases.description: A leading item ('do you love our stunning new earrings?') inflates the yes-rate through wording alone
edge_cases.trigger: brand-flattering or presupposing wording in the question stem
edge_cases.mitigation: rewrite neutral and presupposition-free; move personality to surrounding creative not the item

edge_cases.description: Price buckets overlap ('$20 or less' and '$20-$40' both contain $20) or a category list mixes levels ('earrings' with 'gold hoops')
edge_cases.mitigation: make options mutually exclusive, exhaustive and at one taxonomic level with an explicit opt-out

edge_cases.description: A fixed-order native sticker gives the top option a primacy bump that is read as real preference
edge_cases.trigger: a native sticker's un-randomizable order with a small winning margin
edge_cases.mitigation: counterbalance order across a second post or move off-platform to randomize; discount small fixed-order margins

edge_cases.description: A MaxDiff is attempted inside a single 2-option IG poll sticker and produces an unbalanced, uninterpretable result
edge_cases.trigger: a multi-item forced-trade-off is forced into a binary native format
edge_cases.mitigation: deliver MaxDiff off-platform or approximate with a documented paired-comparison sequence

edge_cases.description: Emoji-slider 0-100 responses are treated as precise interval/ratio data and averaged across separate items
edge_cases.trigger: a one-dimensional VAS is over-interpreted or used to compare distinct items
edge_cases.mitigation: treat the slider as a single-item quasi-interval intensity read, not a cross-item ranking

edge_cases.description: No opt-out is offered, so a respondent who prefers none of the listed categories is forced into a false preference
edge_cases.trigger: a closed item without a none/other/not-sure option
edge_cases.mitigation: always include an explicit none/other/opt-out and monitor its size for a missing option

edge_cases.description: A poll result is used as a market size or 'how many buy' figure
edge_cases.trigger: a responder signal is read as a population count or purchase rate
edge_cases.mitigation: tag the result a [SIGNAL] from a self-selected audience; sizing needs prevalence x frequency and a representative frame (kb2 and the market KBs)

edge_cases.description: A long ranking/rating battery invites straight-lining and non-differentiation that hides real preference differences
edge_cases.trigger: an item battery long enough to trigger satisficing
edge_cases.mitigation: shorten the battery, prefer forced choice, and add an attention/consistency check

edge_cases.description: Price is probed with a single 'would you pay $30?' yes/no and read as a willingness-to-pay curve
edge_cases.trigger: a one-point binary price item is treated as a WTP measurement
edge_cases.mitigation: use Van Westendorp or a Gabor-Granger price ladder for a real WTP read; a single yes/no is one point, not a curve

workflow.action: Name the decision the poll must inform
workflow.description: Write the decision (rank categories/styles to pick the launch 6), the choice set and the action each result triggers
workflow.gate: the decision, choice set and triggered action are written before any instrument is named

workflow.description: State whether the item measures affect, relative preference, intent, WTP, salience or behavior and that liking is not preference/intent/price
workflow.gate: the target construct is named per item with the liking-is-not-demand caveat

workflow.description: Record the IG poll(2)/quiz(<=4)/slider(1D)/question(open) limits and TikTok's removed native poll as dated facts
workflow.gate: the current native ceilings are recorded and dated

workflow.action: Diagnose what the like-poll can and cannot answer
workflow.description: State the CAN (coarse screen) and CANNOT (rank/intensity/intent/WTP/size/which-product) lists for 'do you like earrings?'
workflow.gate: the CAN and CANNOT lists and the screens-not-ranks verdict are stated

workflow.action: Select the instrument via the decision matrix
workflow.description: Map the decision to its instrument (ranking -> MaxDiff/paired-comparison), recording construct and native/off-platform feasibility
workflow.gate: the decision is mapped to an instrument and independent yes/no is rejected for the ranking

workflow.description: Build the best-worst subsets on a balanced incomplete-block design with counting/HB analysis, or a paired-comparison funnel
workflow.gate: a balanced forced-trade-off design yielding a common-scale ranking is specified

workflow.action: Draft neutral questions and MECE options
workflow.description: Write single-barreled non-leading stems and mutually-exclusive, exhaustive, concrete, opt-out-bearing options
workflow.gate: stems are non-leading/single-barreled and options are MECE with an opt-out

workflow.description: Randomize or counterbalance order; where native cannot, swap order across posts or route off-platform
workflow.gate: an order-randomization or counterbalance plan is stated for every closed item

workflow.description: Choose a paired-comparison/staged native sequence or an off-platform MaxDiff/conjoint form and document the trade-off
workflow.gate: the native-sequence-vs-off-platform choice and its sub-audience trade-off are documented

workflow.action: Pretest with cognitive interviews and a soft launch
workflow.description: Think-aloud a few target users and soft-launch to a small slice, inspecting the distribution for pathologies before spend
workflow.gate: a cognitive pretest and soft-launch check precede any paid reach and produce a revised instrument

workflow.description: Assess face/content/construct/criterion validity and test-retest reliability with a hold-out purchase-intent item
workflow.gate: validity against the named construct and a hold-out/stability check are stated

workflow.description: Deliver the recommended instrument set with pretest/validity/signal-tag conditions, stopping before sampling (kb2), reach (kb3) and assortment (S5)
workflow.gate: the instrument set, the four binding conditions and the clean pre-sampling/pre-reach boundary are stated

priority_rationale: The decision framing, measurement target, native affordances and question-type taxonomy come first because every instrument choice depends on the named decision, the construct, the platform ceiling and the type-to-data-type map; the single-choice limits, forced-trade-off logic, MaxDiff, wording/option/order/scale and response-style nodes next, because they are the core craft of what a like-poll can/cannot do and how a valid instrument is built; the attribute/level, conjoint and WTP nodes then extend from single-attribute preference to bundled products and price; and the decision matrix, sequencing, pretest, validity, honesty ledger and hand-off come last because they compose the instrument recommendation, deliver it within the platform constraints, and stop cleanly before sampling (kb2), paid reach (kb3) and assortment (S5).

dominance_rules.rule: The decision dominates the instrument choice
dominance_rules.rationale: an instrument picked from a handy sticker rather than the decision cannot answer the question
dominance_rules.trigger: an instrument is proposed because a platform format is convenient
dominance_rules.action: re-derive the instrument from the named decision and its construct

dominance_rules.rule: A forced trade-off dominates independent yes/no when the decision is to rank
dominance_rules.rationale: independent items let every option score high and produce no ordering
dominance_rules.trigger: multiple categories are polled with independent binary items to rank them
dominance_rules.action: switch to MaxDiff or a paired-comparison funnel that forces a trade-off

dominance_rules.rationale: a high-response but invalid item measures the wrong construct or is biased
dominance_rules.trigger: an easy high-response item is preferred over a valid but harder one
dominance_rules.action: choose the valid instrument and accept lower volume; do not trade validity for taps

dominance_rules.rule: The native affordance ceiling dominates the instrument wishlist
dominance_rules.rationale: no native sticker can host a MaxDiff or conjoint, so wishing does not make it fit
dominance_rules.trigger: a rich instrument is planned for a binary native format
dominance_rules.action: sequence around the ceiling or route off-platform; never fake the instrument in a sticker

dominance_rules.rule: Neutral wording dominates engagement-boosting leading copy
dominance_rules.rationale: a leading stem biases the very signal the poll exists to measure
dominance_rules.trigger: punchy leading copy is proposed for the measured item
dominance_rules.action: keep the item neutral and single-barreled; put personality in surrounding creative

dominance_rules.rule: Affect measurement never dominates a purchase or price question
dominance_rules.rationale: liking is not intent and carries no price
dominance_rules.trigger: a like-poll result is used to claim demand or a price
dominance_rules.action: use an intent or WTP instrument; report the like-poll only as affect

dominance_rules.rule: MECE options with an opt-out dominate a forced false choice
dominance_rules.rationale: omitting an opt-out manufactures a preference from someone who has none
dominance_rules.trigger: a closed item lacks a none/other option
dominance_rules.action: add an explicit opt-out and monitor its share

dominance_rules.rationale: buying reach for a broken item pays to collect uninterpretable answers
dominance_rules.trigger: a poll is scheduled for paid amplification without a pretest
dominance_rules.action: cognitively pretest and soft-launch first; scale only on a clean distribution

anti_rework_rules.rule: Write the decision and construct before choosing any instrument
anti_rework_rules.prevents: building a poll that cannot answer the question and must be rebuilt

anti_rework_rules.rule: Choose a forced trade-off up front when the goal is a ranking
anti_rework_rules.prevents: a folder of independent yes/no polls that cannot be ranked and must be re-fielded

anti_rework_rules.rule: Draft options MECE with an explicit opt-out from the first draft
anti_rework_rules.prevents: re-fielding after discovering overlapping buckets or a forced false choice

anti_rework_rules.rule: Split any attribute-bundling item (category+finish+price) before fielding
anti_rework_rules.prevents: an uninterpretable double-barreled result that has to be discarded and re-asked

anti_rework_rules.rule: Decide native-sequence vs off-platform before building creative
anti_rework_rules.prevents: producing a binary sticker for a job that needs MaxDiff and rebuilding the whole delivery

anti_rework_rules.rule: Cognitively pretest and soft-launch before buying any reach
anti_rework_rules.prevents: paying to collect answers to an ambiguous or leading item

anti_rework_rules.rule: Tag every poll output a [SIGNAL] from responders from the outset, never a [FACT]
anti_rework_rules.prevents: a poll % circulating as measured demand, share or price and having to be retracted

anti_rework_rules.rule: Fix the attribute/level structure before designing a conjoint
anti_rework_rules.prevents: a conjoint with confounded or overlapping attributes whose part-worths must be re-estimated

iteration_protocol.trigger: IG or TikTok changes native poll/quiz/slider mechanics or option counts
iteration_protocol.action: re-inventory the affordances and re-check which instruments are natively feasible or must go off-platform

iteration_protocol.trigger: the pretest or soft launch reveals ambiguous wording, misread options or a distribution pathology
iteration_protocol.action: revise the stems, options and order and re-pretest before scaling

iteration_protocol.trigger: the decision shifts from ranking categories to a priced product configuration
iteration_protocol.action: switch the instrument from MaxDiff to conjoint or a WTP method and re-run the decision map

iteration_protocol.trigger: results show straight-lining, all-yes agreement or non-differentiation
iteration_protocol.action: shorten screens, switch to forced choice and re-check the response-style biases

iteration_protocol.trigger: a hold-out purchase-intent item contradicts the instrument's ranking
iteration_protocol.action: revisit the construct and instrument validity and re-select the instrument if it measured the wrong construct

iteration_protocol.trigger: kb2 reports the responder pool is unrepresentative of the 18-25 buyer
iteration_protocol.action: re-scope the claims the signal can support and add the representativeness caveat to the hand-off

iteration_protocol.trigger: a live off-platform MaxDiff/conjoint tool becomes available or a paired-comparison funnel proves incoherent
iteration_protocol.action: upgrade the delivery from a native sequence to a rigorous off-platform instrument

required_checks: all edge ids unique EDGE_XXX format
all from/to in edges reference valid node ids
all competency_question_refs resolve to valid CQ ids
all evidence_refs resolve to valid source_registry ids
all priority_order entries are valid node ids with no duplicates
high_risk_nodes (risk_if_wrong>=0.80) have non-empty acceptance_tests and human_review_required=true
conflict edges have signed_tension<0 and resolution_rule present
observed_impact=0.0 for all nodes (no observed data)
19-24 nodes, 32-40 edges, 8-10 conflict_axes, 10-12 edge_cases, 9-12 workflow steps
post_formula_checks: all derived fields non-zero after compute run
